purpose: Reconcile the current CALABARZON scope denominator and visible evidence gaps; this is not a completeness claim or biological evidence.
interpretation: The 118 records are named/source-derived research leads in the current file, not proof that every CALABARZON river, spring, lake, reservoir, stream, wetland, estuary, gulf, fishpond, or bay is inventoried.
All 118 current leads have boundaryStatus not-delineated; no boundary geometry was validated by this audit.
Unknown salinity is not freshwater evidence; fish-evidence query gaps or zero search results are not evidence of fish absence.

The October 30 DENR waterbird-site crosswalk adds two aquatic-site leads; the NFRDI Ragay Gulf poster supplies source-reported 2018-2022 species labels but has an image/abstract name conflict and no station-level attribution. No new occurrence assertion, salinity class, geometry, current-presence claim, access claim, or public app record was added.

The Batangas Bay poster crosswalk records nine unconflicted CoL XR species-name matches and one held poster-versus-abstract spelling conflict; these are not independent field identifications, locality assignments, or public species assertions.

The October 30 CC BY fish-checklist batch records 16 historical Ragay Gulf/Ragay Bay type-material treatments and 25 locality groups. A later locality crosswalk anchors Pasacao, Siburio Point, Alibijaban Island and Canmahala Bay at named-place context; it transfers no coordinates, does not assign the whole gulf, and adds no CALABARZON species assertion or public row.

Direct Smithsonian Open Access API metadata reports the exact Canmahala Bay feature name with Camarines Sur in two CC0 invertebrate records. This is historical place-name context only, not fish evidence, a bay boundary, or province/region assignment for the ZooKeys fish lots.

An official NGA Geographic Names Server screen returned no exact Rogo Point name for the Philippines. This bounded gazetteer result does not establish absence or resolve the 1966 locality; the point remains unassigned.

The Guinayangan Water District 2024 Annex J crosswalk adds one surface-water river and seven named or grouped spring-source leads. It provides barangay-level supply context only: no fish records, coordinates, geometry, ecological status, or safety determinations.

The October 30 IIRR watershed brief adds four named Maulawin tributary research leads in Guinayangan. It contains no fish survey and does not provide independently traced channel geometry; the denominator update is not a fish-baseline or completeness claim.

The Kabibihan River System lead is supported by a historical boundary-line issuance, SLSU's 2019 project-completion and 2021 title/authorship listings, a 2021 cross-municipality mollusc-gleaning abstract, and historical mangrove/salinity studies. Viñas River is named by an official 2005 regional bulletin and 2025 NGA sailing directions provide approximate nautical route context; a possible overlap with Hinabaan remains unresolved and the route is not digitized. Neither lead adds finfish species, current water salinity, or validated channel geometry.

The related 2025 conference abstract and 2026 publisher article provide qualitative Lake Sampaloc source-name leads, not a complete inventory or independent replications. The article's diet comments cite external literature and are not local gut-content evidence; its consumption precaution is not a current official advisory. No species, diet, safety/legal, geometry, or public-app row was added.

Caliraya now has a historical largemouth-bass literature cross-check: a secondary 1987 impact narrative, a 1990 literature-survey transcription of an abstract-only historical catch summary, and a 2014 review citing an unretrieved 1989 chapter. This does not establish current occurrence, measured impact, or a local diet profile.

The 2023 AIIB EIA adds 2021-2022 source-reported/observed fish leads for Timalan main stem and Labac, plus non-observations limited to one lower Timbugan segment and one Timalan west-branch location. Fish station allocation, identity methods, and reuse terms remain unresolved; none is a current or complete inventory.

A 2021 Elsevier chapter adds secondary Seven Lakes cluster-level historical fish context and a FARMC personal-communication predation lead, but no per-lake taxa, methods, or measured diet data. No species, occurrence, diet, or app row was added; reuse is not app approval.

A 2023 Springer chapter reports a July-August 2019 gill-net survey across all Seven Lakes and 620 fish samples with per-lake totals. Its taxon-by-lake narrative is partial; the figure-caption red-devil label conflicts with the prose. This is historical research evidence only, not a current checklist or approved public-app dataset.

A 2023 Springer chapter reports a July-August 2019 gill-net survey across all Seven Lakes and 620 fish samples with per-lake totals. Its taxon-by-lake narrative is partial; the figure-caption red-devil label conflicts with the prose. This is historical research evidence only, not a current checklist or approved public-app dataset.

The October 31 PJS full-text follow-up confirms Tayabas River survey methods and a 15-species 2010 aggregate, but the paper conflicts on February wet/dry labeling; item-specific table reuse rights, exact station assignment and current presence remain unresolved.

The October 31 CC BY 4.0 Tikub Lake identity crosswalk records the source-supplied variants Tikob and Ticob and reinforces the Tiaong locality. It does not add fish data: the separate 2014 survey species table remains held for item-specific reuse review.

A bounded public-results search for Ternate Marine Park BMS/BAMS outputs located only the documented monitoring plan and broader coastal-habitat context; no completed fish report was found for Maragondon River Estuary. This is a retrieval gap, not a fish-absence finding.

The October 31 Palanas-name crosswalk distinguishes the 2006 EMB-indexed Palanas River (Naic), a Timalan tributary, from the 1998 Pansipit/Balayan Bay study lead. A 1947 BFAR-hosted Palanas Creek in Lemery may relate to the Batangas study feature, but the identity is unresolved. No route, current legal status, fish evidence or species assertion was added.

The October 31 Geoportal review found publicly described Water Body 1:10,000 and 1:50,000 WMS layers, while the inventory says downloads are temporarily disabled. Empty FeatureInfo responses also occurred at a Taal control point, so no route, feature identity, geometry, or absence conclusion is adopted for Palanas River (Naic).

The 2026-10-31 Palanas River (Naic) GBIF COL XR screen found zero across seven fielded text queries while the Cavite control returned 582; this is not evidence of fish absence, and the river route remains unresolved.

One dated USNM GBIF record for Stolephorus celsior reports Manila Bay, Naic as locality and Manila Bay as waterBody. It is recorded only as a historical shared-bay association, without coordinates or current-presence inference, and is explicitly not assigned to Palanas River.

A separate 2018 OBIS NMNH Fishes archive was checked by exact catalogNumber and otherCatalogNumbers: USNM 204231 was not present in that snapshot. The partial historical archive is not evidence that the specimen is absent from the collection and does not override the distinct 2026 GBIF record.

The AIIB EIA’s February 2020 Naic fisher interviews name grounds around Corregidor and Caballo and separately report five fish and two crab catch labels. The source does not provide species-specific capture coordinates or a marine-waterbody crosswalk; these labels are not assigned to Timalan River, its estuary, or another named waterbody.

The October 31 Catalog of Fishes crosswalk proposes a spelling correction for the EIA’s Ratrilliger brachysoma and maps Valamugil seheli to the Catalog’s current Moolgarda seheli combination. These are name-indexing results only: they do not validate interview fish identifications or resolve capture grounds, and no waterbody assertion was added.

The 2017 NFRDI Manila Bay trawl paper names hairtail, black pomfret and common ponyfish as more abundant in its southern sector near Corregidor. Its 42-species Corregidor count is part of a fish-and-invertebrate survey; no per-taxon station/date crosswalk or item-specific table reuse was established. This remains historical regional research context, not a current occurrence or public checklist.
